topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on dental education curriculum design. Findings may not transfer directly to other professional disciplines or non-healthcare sectors, though the competency framework methodology could be adapted.
takeaways: Consider developing role-specific AI competency frameworks for your sector rather than adopting generic AI literacy models — dental education's example shows how discipline-specific skills (e.g., AI in diagnostics, treatment planning) differ from general AI knowledge.

Embed AI literacy into professional qualification standards early (undergraduate level) to normalise AI as a core capability rather than treating it as optional upskilling for established practitioners.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Likely global in scope given Frontiers' international reach, but generalisability depends on whether the review covers diverse educational contexts and sectors. Limited detail in snippet to assess fully.
takeaways: Identify specific AI competency gaps in your organisation's workforce by mapping current skills against emerging roles that require AI literacy — this can help prioritise which competencies to develop first.

Consider multi-layered learning approaches (technical skills, critical thinking, ethical reasoning) rather than technical training alone, as higher education models suggest integrated development yields stronger competency outcomes.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education sector; applicability to other organisational contexts and non-academic settings requires adaptation of the four-domain model.
takeaways: AI literacy functions as a meta-skill that integrates technical, critical thinking, ethical, and organisational dimensions — use this four-domain framework to design comprehensive AI capability programs rather than treating technical skills in isolation.

For academic leaders and managers, develop AI literacy through domain-specific applications (e.g., research management, curriculum design, administrative automation) rather than abstract AI concepts to increase relevance and uptake.
Assess your organisation's current AI literacy across all four domains to identify capability gaps; focus development efforts on weaker domains that constrain effective AI adoption and innovation.

articles.title: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports  Nature
articles.sample: Higher vocational education sector (specific geography not specified from snippet)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings are based on vocational education context and may not fully transfer to corporate workforce training or general adult populations. Geographic scope unclear from snippet provided.
takeaways: A competency-based 'ladder pathway' approach can structure AI literacy development in stages, allowing learners to progress systematically rather than attempting comprehensive AI knowledge all at once.
Validation of this pathway model suggests organisations can adopt stepped competency frameworks to design targeted AI upskilling programmes tailored to learner readiness and prior knowledge.
Consider assessing your workforce's current AI literacy level using validated competency frameworks before designing training, rather than assuming uniform starting points across employees.

articles.title: US Department of Labor promotes AI literacy across the American workforce - U.S. Department of Labor (.gov)
articles.snippet: US Department of Labor promotes AI literacy across the American workforce  U.S. Department of Labor (.gov)
articles.generalisability: US-specific — describes US Department of Labor initiatives, federal funding programmes, and US workforce policy that do not apply in Australia. Australian organisations would need to identify equivalent local resources and government support mechanisms.
takeaways: US-specific: The Department of Labor offers federal grants and partnerships for AI literacy training — Australian organisations should investigate equivalent state and federal funding through relevant Australian agencies (e.g. National Skills Commission, industry bodies).

The initiative emphasises sectoral and demographic reach across the American workforce — consider mapping your own organisation's skill gaps by role, age, and department to target AI literacy interventions where they matter most.

Government-backed AI literacy programmes signal growing workforce demand for these skills — prioritise baseline AI literacy training before moving to advanced technical upskilling to build organisational readiness.

articles.title: The influence of employability skills on quality of employment in AI-driven labour market transformations: the roles of academic achievement and motivation - Nature
articles.snippet: The influence of employability skills on quality of employment in AI-driven labour market transformations: the roles of academic achievement and motivation  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and geographic scope — these details are not evident from the title and snippet provided. Further assessment requires access to the full methodology.
takeaways: Employability skills appear to mediate the relationship between academic achievement and employment quality in AI-transformed roles — focus upskilling programmes on practical capabilities, not credentials alone.

Motivation emerges as a key moderating factor; employees with higher motivation may translate employability skills into better employment outcomes — consider motivation assessment and cultivation alongside technical AI literacy.

Quality of employment (not just job placement) is the relevant outcome measure in AI-driven labour markets — when designing AI capability programmes, track role fit, job satisfaction, and career progression, not just employment rates.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not detailed in snippet. The study examines moderating mechanisms (self-efficacy and transformational leadership) that are likely relevant across contexts, but geographic scope, sector, and sample size are unclear from the title alone.
takeaways: Leaders can mitigate AI-driven job insecurity by demonstrating transformational leadership behaviours — focus on inspiring vision, individualised support, and intellectual stimulation to help employees see themselves as adaptable to technological change.

Invest in building employee self-efficacy around AI tools and upskilling; employees with stronger confidence in their ability to learn and work with AI experience less job insecurity when AI is introduced.

AI implementation should be paired with leadership development and capability-building programs rather than treated as a technical-only change — the human factors of leadership quality and employee confidence directly buffer against negative psychological outcomes.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings on paternalistic leadership effects may be most relevant to Asian organizational contexts where this leadership style is more prevalent; generalisability to Western management approaches unclear without full article review.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customizing or 'crafting' AI systems to fit their work — this autonomy can strengthen their willingness to collaborate with AI rather than resist it.

Under paternalistic leadership styles, emphasize how AI adoption serves employees' long-term development and organizational welfare to activate psychological ownership; framing matters for engagement.

Design AI implementation strategies that allow employees input into how AI is configured or deployed in their workflows, as this sense of ownership may be a key lever for driving adoption and collaboration.

articles.title: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents strategic argument based on business logic rather than empirical research; applies broadly to knowledge-work sectors but lacks quantitative evidence of long-term outcomes.
takeaways: Prioritise AI augmentation (enhancing human capability) over full automation in roles requiring judgment, creativity, or stakeholder trust — this preserves institutional knowledge and employee engagement while building sustainable competitive advantage.

Design AI implementation to upskill existing teams rather than replace them; this reduces workforce disruption, maintains organisational culture, and positions employees as AI-capable contributors rather than redundant roles.
Evaluate AI adoption through a capability-building lens: assess whether the technology expands what your workforce can do, rather than asking only whether it reduces headcount or cost.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — geographic scope and sample characteristics not evident. Generalisability depends on study design and participant demographics not provided in the title/snippet alone.
takeaways: Psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) may be a key lever for helping employees innovate when AI tools are introduced; consider assessing and building these capacities in staff alongside AI upskilling.
Frame AI systems as job resources (tools that expand capability) rather than threats; this reframing may unlock stronger engagement and innovation outcomes from teams working alongside algorithms.
Monitor whether high-performing employees in algorithm-driven roles are sustaining their psychological capital over time, or experiencing erosion due to surveillance, pacing, or autonomy loss.

articles.title: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot be fully assessed from title and snippet alone. Generalisability depends on sample composition, industry sectors, and geographic scope, which are not evident from the provided information.
takeaways: Employee-AI collaboration can boost work engagement through two distinct psychological mechanisms — identify which pathway is most relevant to your workforce (e.g., competence/autonomy vs. social connection) and design collaboration workflows accordingly.

When implementing AI tools, explicitly map how they address psychological needs; misalignment between tool design and employee motivations may limit engagement gains even when technical capabilities are strong.

articles.title: Why AI Boosts Creativity for Some Employees but Not Others - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why AI Boosts Creativity for Some Employees but Not Others  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on expert commentary rather than empirical research. Findings likely reflect patterns in knowledge-work sectors but lack geographic specificity and may not generalise to all employee populations or industries.
takeaways: Assess individual differences in AI comfort and cognitive style when rolling out AI tools; employees with lower AI familiarity or those prone to cognitive rigidity may need targeted support to leverage AI creatively rather than defaulting to routine task automation.

Design implementation strategies that encourage experimentation and reframing of problems with AI as a thinking partner, not just a productivity tool, to unlock creative potential across your workforce.

Consider pairing AI tool adoption with training that emphasises divergent thinking and exploration, since some employees may naturally constrain AI use to incremental improvements unless explicitly encouraged to think expansively.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full article — depends on sample size, industry sectors, and geographic scope of organisations studied. Approach-avoidance framework may vary by cultural context and AI maturity levels.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger two opposing employee responses: approach behaviours (seeking new skills, redesigning tasks for AI collaboration) and avoidance behaviours (withdrawing effort, resisting upskilling). Recognise which response your team exhibits and design targeted interventions — e.g. early wins and skill-building for avoiders, growth opportunities for approachers.

Job crafting (how employees reshape their own roles) is a critical lever during AI transitions. Create explicit permission and psychological safety for employees to redesign their work around AI tools rather than passively accepting top-down role changes.

Use this model to diagnose adoption resistance: if employees are avoiding rather than approaching, address underlying threat perception (job security, skill gaps, autonomy loss) before expecting productive job redesign.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical data or geographic scope. Findings and recommendations may reflect US-centric business school viewpoint and may not directly translate to Australian organisational contexts.
takeaways: Identify which work tasks in your organisation are most susceptible to AI disruption, then design targeted upskilling programs for affected teams before displacement occurs rather than reactively.

Use this period of AI transition to clarify your organisation's values and culture — employees undergoing change are more receptive to messaging about how AI aligns with (or challenges) your organisational purpose.
Create early-adopter roles or pilot groups who experiment with AI tools and model new ways of working, reducing fear and creating peer-to-peer learning pathways across the workforce.

articles.title: Advancing applied behavioral science: the GAP framework - Nature
articles.snippet: Advancing applied behavioral science: the GAP framework  Nature
articles.generalisability: High-level framework applicable across contexts, though specific examples and case studies would determine relevance to Australian organisational settings.
takeaways: The GAP framework (Goals, Actions, Persons) provides a structured approach to designing behaviour change interventions — map desired outcomes, identify specific actions required, and segment populations by relevant characteristics before implementation.

Applied behavioural science succeeds when interventions target the right audience with the right action at the right time; avoid one-size-fits-all approaches and instead tailor interventions based on who needs to change and what specific behaviour matters most.

Use the framework to diagnose why behaviour change efforts fail — misaligned goals, poorly designed actions, or targeting the wrong population segments — before scaling interventions across your organisation.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on BCG's consulting experience across clients, but specific case studies and client contexts are not detailed in the snippet provided. Findings may reflect larger multinational organisations more than SMEs.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge first, not a technology implementation — success depends on how effectively you help employees transition roles and develop new skills alongside system rollout.

Plan for workforce transformation in parallel with AI deployment: identify which roles will change, which skills become obsolete, and what new capabilities teams need, rather than treating technology and people change as separate workstreams.

articles.title: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Companies That Choose AI Augmentation Over Automation May Win in the Long Run  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents strategic perspective on AI implementation approaches, but lacks empirical evidence or case studies to support claims about long-term competitive outcomes. Applicability depends on organisational context and sector.
takeaways: Design AI implementations around augmenting employee capabilities rather than replacing roles—this approach may improve employee buy-in and retention while preserving institutional knowledge.

When planning AI adoption, explicitly evaluate whether augmentation or automation better serves your long-term business objectives, workforce stability, and competitive positioning before making implementation choices.

articles.title: Reconfiguring work: Change management in the age of gen AI - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Reconfiguring work: Change management in the age of gen AI  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across multiple industries and geographies, but findings reflect primarily large enterprise contexts and may not fully apply to small-to-medium organisations or specific regional labour markets like Australia.
takeaways: Design change management strategies that treat gen AI adoption as a reconfiguration of work roles rather than simple tool implementation — this requires deliberate attention to which tasks are being redistributed, eliminated, or created, and clear communication about how individual roles will evolve.

Establish cross-functional sponsorship and change champions who can help employees make sense of AI's impact on their day-to-day work; resistance often stems from uncertainty about job security and capability gaps, which can be mitigated through transparent upskilling pathways and role redesign conversations.

Map and sequence change interventions around three critical junctures: awareness-building about AI's organisational strategy, skills development before implementation, and post-rollout reinforcement — bundling these together is more effective than reactive, post-launch training.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline-driven summary of neuroimaging research without detail on sample size, methodology, or replication status. Original study details not provided in snippet.
takeaways: Brain imaging can detect structural or functional differences linked to psychopathic traits, suggesting neurobiology influences personality variation rather than behaviour being purely learned.

The framing of findings as 'shocking' reflects how brain science fascinates the public, even when effects are modest or correlational — a reminder that neuroimaging headlines often overstate certainty.
Psychopathy exists on a spectrum in the general population, not just in criminal settings, which challenges the stereotype that it's rare or exclusively dangerous.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — geographic scope and sample characteristics not specified. Findings depend on wine review dataset composition and whether patterns hold across different cultures' wine-drinking and review-writing practices.
takeaways: Language patterns in how people describe wine (word choice, descriptors, emotional tone) can reveal underlying personality traits — a fun example of how AI can spot personality signals in everyday writing.
Wine reviews are more psychologically interesting than they might seem: what you focus on when tasting (acidity vs. emotion, technical vs. sensory) says something real about who you are.
This highlights a counterintuitive insight: hobbies and leisure activities produce rich personality data simply because people write more freely and authentically about things they love.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear — the snippet provides no information about sample size, geography, methodology, or study details, making it impossible to assess generalisability.
takeaways: A counterintuitive finding: an overactive thyroid is linked to darker personality traits (narcissism, psychopathy, or Machiavellianism), suggesting physical health conditions can correlate with personality expression in surprising ways.

This opens a curious question about cause and effect — does thyroid dysfunction influence personality, or do people with certain personality profiles engage in behaviours that affect thyroid function?
A reminder that personality isn't purely psychological: biology, endocrinology, and other bodily systems might shape how we present ourselves to the world in ways we rarely consider.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition (country, demographics); twin studies typically use convenience samples that may not represent broader populations, though the methodology allows for genetic-environmental decomposition.
takeaways: Twin studies reveal that authoritarian beliefs have a measurable genetic component — not purely learned or environmentally determined — challenging the assumption that political ideology is entirely shaped by upbringing or experience.

The 'surprising roots' likely refer to the counterintuitive finding that genetic factors influence personality traits (like preference for order or discomfort with ambiguity) that predispose people toward authoritarianism, rather than genes directly coding for political views.
This research highlights why people with similar upbringings can diverge sharply in political beliefs — genetic differences in temperament and risk tolerance play a hidden role in shaping ideology.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reviews existing research on MBTI validity, but findings depend heavily on the quality and scope of studies included; MBTI's predictive power varies significantly across different leadership contexts and outcome measures.
takeaways: The Myers-Briggs test is surprisingly poor at predicting actual leadership behaviours — despite its enormous popularity in corporate settings, the scientific evidence for its predictive validity is weak and inconsistent.

Why this matters: millions of employees take MBTI assessments annually for leadership development and team-building, yet the personality categories it creates don't reliably forecast who'll be an effective leader or how teams will actually perform together.

The gap between MBTI's cultural ubiquity and scientific credibility reveals how readily intuitive-sounding personality frameworks become institutionalised in workplaces without robust evidence backing their claims.

articles.title: New relationships take a surprising physical toll on older adults - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New relationships take a surprising physical toll on older adults  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full article — appears to be reporting on a specific study, but scope and sample characteristics are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: The counterintuitive finding that new romantic relationships can temporarily worsen physical health in older adults challenges the common assumption that romance is universally beneficial.
New relationships apparently demand cognitive and emotional energy that may affect sleep, stress levels, or health behaviours — a reminder that life transitions affect the body, not just the mind.
This suggests the experience of falling in love late in life involves measurable biological changes, making romance a genuinely embodied experience across all ages.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — appears to focus on academic teams in multicultural settings, but geographic scope and sample size cannot be determined from the title alone. Findings may have limited applicability beyond higher education contexts.
takeaways: AI tools can be designed to support inclusive leadership practices that mitigate gender biases in team dynamics — consider how algorithmic prompts or decision-support systems might help leaders recognise and address gendered participation patterns in your own teams.

In multicultural academic (or knowledge-work) teams, algorithmic assistance paired with intentional leadership may reduce the psychological burden on underrepresented members to 'speak up', potentially strengthening psychological safety.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad global scope, but generalisability depends on PwC's sampling methodology and respondent demographics, which are not detailed in the snippet. Results likely skew toward white-collar and professional sectors given PwC's client base.
takeaways: Use this survey to benchmark your organisation's psychological safety climate against global workforce sentiment — identify gaps where employees' hopes and fears diverge from your current culture to prioritise safety interventions.

The survey data can inform dialogue with leadership about which fears are most prevalent in your workforce, helping you make a case for targeted psychological safety initiatives rather than generic culture programs.
Compare results across your own employee segments (level, tenure, function) to uncover where psychological safety is weakest and design interventions for high-risk groups.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — article abstract does not provide sample size, geography, or sector details. Findings may be context-dependent and require replication across different organisational settings and geographies before broad application.
takeaways: AI adoption without concurrent investment in psychological safety and ethical leadership can increase employee depression risk — prioritise these cultural foundations before or alongside technology implementation.
Ethical leadership is a critical moderator of AI adoption impact; leaders must explicitly model ethical AI use and create norms that protect employee wellbeing during organisational transitions.
Measure psychological safety proactively during AI rollouts; low safety signals may indicate emerging mental health risks that require immediate intervention, not just technical adjustment.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG research likely draws on global consulting experience and client data, but specific sample composition, methodology, and geographic distribution are not detailed in the snippet.
takeaways: Create explicit team norms that invite questions, dissent, and error reporting without fear of repercussion — this reduces information asymmetries and gives quieter or junior employees equal voice in problem-solving.

Measure psychological safety alongside performance metrics; teams with high safety show better innovation and retention, making it a lever for addressing equity gaps across different employee demographics.
Leaders should model vulnerability and curiosity (asking for help, admitting mistakes) rather than projecting invulnerability — this signals that speaking up is genuinely safe and expected.

articles.title: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety - Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.source: Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.snippet: Debunking misconceptions about workplace psychological safety  Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents conceptual clarifications from a US academic institution but does not report empirical data; applicability depends on whether misconceptions identified are universal or US-centric.
takeaways: Identify and challenge common false beliefs about psychological safety in your workplace (e.g., that it means avoiding all conflict or that it requires universal agreement) so leaders and teams develop a more accurate mental model.

Use clarified definitions of psychological safety to diagnose whether your organisation's actual barriers are conceptual misunderstandings, structural blockers, or leadership behaviour—each requires different interventions.

articles.title: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — likely reflects patterns in knowledge-work sectors in developed economies, but lacks empirical data on scope and may not generalise to all industries or regions.
takeaways: Identify and address the specific fears driving non-disclosure (e.g., job security, performance evaluation concerns, perceived rule-breaking) — employees won't be transparent if they fear punishment or misunderstanding.

Establish clear, written policies on acceptable AI use and explicitly signal that disclosure is safe and expected; without this psychological safety foundation, transparency remains low regardless of monitoring or enforcement.

Create low-stakes channels for employees to report AI usage (e.g., regular check-ins, anonymous surveys, team discussions) and demonstrate through visible leadership behaviour that disclosure leads to support, not consequences.
